etymology: From oneness (the denial of the three Persons) and Pentecostalism; a modalist movement arising out of early twentieth-century Pentecostalism.
biblical_def: Oneness Pentecostalism is a modalist movement that arose out of early twentieth-century Pentecostalism, denying the doctrine of the Trinity and teaching instead that God is a single Person who has manifested Himself in three successive modes or roles—as Father in creation, as Son in redemption, and as Holy Spirit in the church age. It holds that “Jesus” is the one name of the one God, and accordingly baptizes only in the name of Jesus rather than in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost as the Lord commanded. Many of its bodies further teach that speaking in tongues is the necessary evidence of salvation and impose a rigorous code of outward standards. Measured against Scripture and the creeds, Oneness doctrine is a revival of the ancient heresy of Sabellianism or modalism, condemned by the early church. The Bible reveals not one Person in three masks but three distinct Persons in one undivided Godhead: the Father sends the Son, the Son prays to the Father and is not the Father, the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and all three appear distinctly at Christ’s baptism. The dictionary names Oneness Pentecostalism as a serious doctrinal error—a denial of the Trinity, the foundational doctrine of the Christian faith—and holds with the whole church catholic that the one God eternally exists as three coequal, coeternal, distinct Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
webster_summary: A modalist movement from early Pentecostalism denying the Trinity, teaching one Person in three successive modes; a revival of ancient Sabellianism, condemned by the church.
webster_full: ONENESS PENTECOSTALISM, a modalist movement denying the doctrine of the Trinity.
Teaches one Person manifested in three modes: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Baptizes only in the name of Jesus, against Christ’s Trinitarian command.
A revival of ancient Sabellianism (modalism), condemned by the early church.
Rejected by Scripture, which reveals three distinct Persons in one Godhead.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Joh 17:5
And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.
Mat 3:16
And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:
corruption_summary: Oneness Pentecostalism denies the Trinity, collapsing the three Persons into one Person wearing three masks.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the denial of the Trinity itself, the foundation of the Christian faith. By teaching that Father, Son, and Spirit are not three distinct Persons but three roles of one Person, Oneness doctrine revives the modalism of Sabellius that the early church condemned. Scripture forbids it: the Word was with God and was God; the Son prayed to the Father and spoke of the glory He shared with Him before the world was; the three appeared distinctly when the Son stood in the water, the Spirit descended as a dove, and the Father spoke from heaven. One Person cannot send Himself, pray to Himself, and proceed from Himself.

The error issues in further corruptions: the rejection of the Trinitarian baptismal formula Christ commanded, the making of tongues a test of salvation, and a legalism of outward standards. The dictionary names the movement plainly as heterodox—outside the bounds of Trinitarian orthodoxy held by the whole church catholic from Nicaea onward. The one true God eternally subsists as three coequal, coeternal, distinct Persons; to deny this is to deny the God who has revealed Himself, and the gospel that depends upon the Father sending the Son and the Spirit applying His work.
roots_summary: The movement’s name marks its central error—a “oneness” that denies the three Persons of the Godhead.
roots_lines: “Oneness” — the denial of the tri-personal God for a single-Person deity.
Modalism (Sabellianism) — the ancient heresy of God in successive modes, here revived.
Greek hen — one; the movement absolutizes God’s unity against His tri-personality.
“Jesus only” baptism — against the Trinitarian formula of Matthew 28:19.
Condemned by the Nicene faith of the whole church catholic.
usage: Oneness Pentecostalism is identified as a modern revival of modalism.
Its “Jesus only” baptism is contrasted with Christ’s Trinitarian command.
It is named as a denial of the Trinity, outside Christian orthodoxy.

etymology: From Jehovah (the divine name) and witnesses; the name adopted by the movement founded in the late nineteenth century under Charles Taze Russell.
biblical_def: Jehovah’s Witnesses are a movement founded in the late nineteenth century out of the teaching of Charles Taze Russell and organized through the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, which, despite using the Scriptures and the divine name Jehovah, denies the central doctrines of the Christian faith. They deny the Trinity, teaching that Jehovah is a single Person; they deny the full deity of Christ, holding Him to be a created being, the first and highest of Jehovah’s creatures, identified with the archangel Michael; they deny the personality and deity of the Holy Spirit, reducing Him to an impersonal active force; and they deny the bodily resurrection of Christ and the conscious eternal punishment of the wicked, teaching annihilation instead. Their own translation of Scripture, the New World Translation, alters key texts to support these denials, rendering John 1:1 “the Word was a god.” Measured against the Bible and the historic faith, these teachings revive ancient errors—the Arianism condemned at Nicaea above all—and place the movement outside Christian orthodoxy. The dictionary names Jehovah’s Witnesses as a non-Christian sect, however sincere and zealous its members, for it denies the deity of Christ, the Trinity, and salvation by grace. The true witnesses to Jehovah confess Jesus Christ as Lord and God, the eternal Son made flesh, before whom every knee shall bow; the gospel hangs upon the very deity this movement denies.
webster_summary: A movement founded under C. T. Russell, organized as the Watch Tower Society, which denies the Trinity, the deity of Christ, the personal Holy Spirit, and eternal punishment—a revival of Arianism outside Christian orthodoxy.
webster_full: JEHOVAH’S WITNESSES, a movement founded under Charles Taze Russell.
Organized through the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society.
Denies the Trinity and the full deity of Christ, making Him a created being.
Denies the personality of the Holy Spirit and teaches annihilation of the wicked.
A revival of Arianism, placed outside Christian orthodoxy.
scriptures: Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Col 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
Tit 2:13
Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;
corruption_summary: Jehovah’s Witnesses deny the deity of Christ and the Trinity, reviving the Arian heresy condemned at Nicaea.
corruption_paragraphs: The central corruption is the denial of the full deity of Christ—the ancient Arian error that the Son is a creature, the highest of created beings, but not true God. The movement’s own translation mistranslates John 1:1 to read “the Word was a god,” against the plain Greek and the witness of the whole New Testament. But Thomas confessed the risen Christ as “My Lord and my God”; in Christ dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily; and Scripture calls Him “the great God and our Saviour.” To make the Son a creature is to overthrow the gospel, for no creature could bear the infinite weight of divine justice.

From this root spring further denials: of the Trinity, of the personal Holy Spirit, of Christ’s bodily resurrection, and of eternal conscious punishment, replaced by annihilationism. The dictionary names Jehovah’s Witnesses, with all respect for the sincerity of individual members, as a non-Christian sect outside the bounds of the historic faith. Its very name claims to witness to Jehovah, yet it denies the Lord Jesus Christ who is Himself Jehovah the Son; the true witness to God confesses the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God in three Persons, and bows to Christ as Lord and God.
roots_summary: The movement’s name claims to witness to Jehovah, yet its doctrine denies the deity of Jehovah the Son.
roots_lines: “Jehovah” — the divine name the movement uses while denying Christ’s deity.
Arianism — the ancient heresy, condemned at Nicaea, that the Son is a creature.
The New World Translation — their altered Bible, mistranslating John 1:1.
Christ identified with the archangel Michael, against His eternal deity.
Annihilationism — their denial of eternal conscious punishment.
usage: Jehovah’s Witnesses are identified as a modern revival of Arianism.
Their mistranslation of John 1:1 is answered by the deity of Christ throughout Scripture.
They are named a non-Christian sect for denying the Trinity and Christ’s deity.

etymology: From decisional (resting on a human decision) and regeneration; a modern error that grounds the new birth in the sinner’s act of will.
biblical_def: Decisional regeneration is the modern revivalist error that grounds the new birth in the sinner’s own act of decision—teaching that a man is born again by making a choice for Christ, walking an aisle, raising a hand, signing a card, or praying a prescribed prayer, so that regeneration is treated as the effect and reward of the human will rather than the sovereign and prior work of God. It reverses the biblical order of salvation. Scripture teaches that regeneration is the cause of faith, not its effect: the new birth is of God, who quickens the dead, gives the new heart, and grants repentance and faith as His gifts. Men are born again “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God”; the natural man is dead in trespasses, unable to come to Christ except the Father draw him. The decision a true convert makes is real, but it is the fruit of regeneration already wrought by the Spirit, not its cause. Decisional regeneration, by contrast, makes the sinner the author of his own new birth and breeds a harvest of false assurance, treating the recitation of a prayer or the walking of an aisle as proof of conversion apart from the fruit of a changed life. The dictionary names decisional regeneration as a serious error that has filled the churches with unconverted members confident of a salvation they never received: the new birth is the work of God, sovereign and effectual, and the evidence of it is not a past decision but present and persevering faith, repentance, and holiness.
webster_summary: The revivalist error grounding the new birth in the sinner’s decision—an aisle walked, a prayer prayed—reversing the biblical order, which makes regeneration the sovereign cause of faith, not its effect.
webster_full: DECISIONAL REGENERATION, the error grounding the new birth in the sinner’s decision.
Treats regeneration as the reward of a human choice, aisle-walk, or prayer.
Reverses the biblical order: regeneration is the cause of faith, not its effect.
Men are born again “not of the will of man, but of God.”
Breeds false assurance in those who trust a past decision apart from a changed life.
scriptures: Joh 1:13
Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
Joh 3:8
The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
Eph 2:1
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
corruption_summary: Decisional regeneration makes the sinner the author of his own new birth and breeds false assurance from a mere decision.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the reversal of the order of salvation. Scripture makes regeneration the sovereign, prior work of God that produces faith; decisional regeneration makes the human decision the cause that produces the new birth. But the dead cannot raise themselves, and the natural man cannot come to Christ except the Father draw him. To be born again is to be born “not of the will of man, but of God”; the new birth is as much beyond the sinner’s power and choice as the wind is beyond his command. The decision a convert makes is the fruit of the Spirit’s prior work, never its cause.

The practical fruit of the error is a harvest of false assurance. Multitudes have been told they were saved the moment they prayed a prayer or walked an aisle, and have rested ever since on that act, though no fruit of repentance, faith, or holiness followed. The dictionary names this as a deadly corruption: it fills the church with unconverted members confident of heaven, and it dishonors the sovereign grace of God by crediting the new birth to the creature’s will. True conversion is the work of God, and its evidence is not a remembered decision but a present and persevering faith that bears the fruit of a transformed life.
roots_summary: The phrase names the error of crediting the new birth to a human decision, against the sovereign and prior work of God.
roots_lines: “Decisional” — resting the new birth on the sinner’s act of will.
Greek gennao anōthen — to be born from above, born again, a work of God.
The biblical order: regeneration precedes and produces faith and repentance.
Set against the “sinner’s prayer” treated as the cause of conversion.
Allied with the decline from the older doctrine of effectual calling.
usage: Decisional regeneration is named as a reversal of the biblical order of salvation.
It is set against effectual calling and the sovereignty of God in the new birth.
It is cited as a chief source of false assurance in modern churches.

etymology: From trajectory (a path of movement toward a goal) and hermeneutic (a method of interpretation); a method that reads Scripture as pointing beyond its own commands.
biblical_def: The trajectory hermeneutic—also called the redemptive-movement hermeneutic—is a method of interpreting Scripture which claims that the Bible’s commands are not its final word, but mark points along a moral trajectory that the church must continue beyond the text itself. On this method, the interpreter discerns the direction in which Scripture was supposedly moving—toward greater freedom, equality, or inclusion—and then extends that movement past what the Bible actually commands, so that the church may sanction today what the apostles forbade. It has been used chiefly to overturn the Bible’s teaching on the roles of men and women, and from there to argue for the acceptance of what Scripture plainly condemns. The dictionary names the trajectory hermeneutic as a corruption of the doctrine of Scripture, for it sets the interpreter’s sense of where the Bible was heading above the Bible’s own words, making the commands of God provisional and the church the judge of which to keep. Scripture does not present itself as a launching-point to be left behind but as the final and sufficient rule of faith and life, not to be added to or subtracted from. Where the apostles ground their commands in creation, not culture—“Adam was first formed, then Eve”—there is no trajectory beyond the text to be found. The method is in truth a way of escaping the authority of Scripture while still claiming its name; the dictionary holds the written Word as the abiding and unchangeable standard, its commands binding because God has spoken them.
webster_summary: A method claiming Scripture’s commands mark points on a moral trajectory the church must extend beyond the text—a corruption of biblical authority used to overturn what the apostles forbade.
webster_full: TRAJECTORY HERMENEUTIC, a method reading Scripture as pointing beyond its own commands.
Also called the redemptive-movement hermeneutic.
Claims the church must extend the Bible’s supposed direction past what it actually commands.
Used to overturn Scripture’s teaching on the roles of men and women, and more.
Sets the interpreter’s sense of direction above the Bible’s own final words.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book:
For Adam was first formed, then Eve.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
corruption_summary: The trajectory method makes God’s commands provisional, setting the interpreter’s sense of direction above the written Word.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is an assault on the authority and finality of Scripture. By treating the Bible’s commands as mere stages along a trajectory to be extended beyond the text, the method makes the written Word provisional and the interpreter the judge of which commands still bind. But Scripture presents itself as the final and sufficient rule, not a launching-point to be left behind; it forbids adding to or subtracting from the words of God, and declares that the word of our God shall stand for ever. To extend a supposed trajectory past the text is to add to Scripture under the pretense of fulfilling it.

The method is used chiefly to overturn what Scripture plainly teaches—first the ordered roles of men and women, then, in the hands of others, the biblical sexual ethic itself. Yet where the apostles ground their commands, they ground them not in passing culture but in creation: “Adam was first formed, then Eve.” There is no trajectory beyond a command rooted in the unchangeable order of creation. The dictionary names the trajectory hermeneutic as a sophisticated way of escaping the authority of Scripture while still claiming its name, and holds the written Word as the abiding, sufficient, and unchangeable standard of faith and life.
roots_summary: The phrase names a method that reads Scripture’s commands as way-stations to be surpassed, against the finality of the written Word.
roots_lines: “Trajectory” — a supposed path of moral movement beyond the text.
Also “redemptive-movement hermeneutic.”
Greek hermēneuō — to interpret; the method is one of interpretation.
Set against the sufficiency and finality of Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16-17).
Apostolic commands grounded in creation leave no trajectory beyond the text.
usage: The trajectory hermeneutic is named as a corruption of biblical authority.
It is answered by the apostles’ grounding of commands in creation, not culture.
The finality and sufficiency of Scripture are set against extending its commands.

etymology: From Toronto (the city of its origin) and blessing; a charismatic revival movement of the mid-1990s.
biblical_def: The Toronto Blessing was a charismatic revival movement that began in the mid-1990s at a church near the Toronto airport and spread widely, marked by extraordinary physical phenomena attributed to the Holy Spirit—uncontrollable laughter, falling to the ground, shaking, weeping, and even animal sounds such as roaring and barking. Its defenders hailed these manifestations as a fresh outpouring of the Spirit; its critics, including many within the broader charismatic world, judged them to be disorderly and without scriptural warrant. Measured by the Word, the movement illustrates the danger of seeking and validating spiritual experience apart from the test of Scripture. The Bible nowhere presents such uncontrolled phenomena as marks of the Spirit’s work; on the contrary, the Spirit is the author not of confusion but of peace, the fruit of the Spirit includes self-control and temperance, and all things in the assembly are to be done decently and in order. The true and abiding works of the Spirit are conviction of sin, the exaltation of Christ, the love of the truth, growth in holiness, and the fruit of love, joy, peace, and the rest—none of which is measured by physical sensation or ecstatic display. The dictionary names the Toronto Blessing as a cautionary instance of experience-driven religion divorced from the Word: spiritual phenomena, however intense, are not self-authenticating, and every spirit must be tried whether it be of God. The Spirit’s genuine work always honors Christ, accords with Scripture, and bears the orderly fruit of holiness, not the spectacle of the flesh.
webster_summary: A mid-1990s charismatic revival marked by uncontrolled laughter, falling, shaking, and animal sounds—a cautionary case of experience-driven religion divorced from the Word and the Spirit’s orderly fruit.
webster_full: TORONTO BLESSING, a charismatic revival movement of the mid-1990s.
Began at a church near the Toronto airport and spread widely.
Marked by uncontrolled laughter, falling, shaking, weeping, and animal sounds.
Hailed by defenders as an outpouring of the Spirit; judged by critics as disorderly.
A cautionary case of seeking spiritual experience apart from the test of Scripture.
scriptures: For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Gal 5:22
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
corruption_summary: Spiritual experience is sought and validated apart from Scripture, mistaking uncontrolled phenomena for the Spirit’s work.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the validating of spiritual experience apart from the test of the Word. The uncontrolled laughter, falling, shaking, and animal noises of the movement were taken as self-evident marks of the Spirit, though Scripture nowhere presents such phenomena as His work. But the Spirit is the author not of confusion but of peace; His fruit includes temperance and self-control; and all things in the assembly are to be done decently and in order. Phenomena that overthrow self-control and decorum bear the marks of the flesh or worse, not of the Spirit of order.

The dictionary names the Toronto Blessing as a cautionary instance of experience-driven religion, while distinguishing it from the genuine, abiding works of the Spirit. The true marks of the Spirit’s presence are conviction of sin, the exaltation of Christ, love of the truth, growth in holiness, and the orderly fruit of love, joy, and peace—none measured by physical sensation. John commands that the spirits be tried whether they are of God; intensity of feeling is no proof of divine origin. The remedy is not to quench the Spirit but to test every claimed manifestation by the Word, which honors Christ and produces holiness, not spectacle.
roots_summary: The movement’s name marks its origin and its claim; the dictionary tests its phenomena by the Spirit’s orderly fruit.
roots_lines: “Toronto” — the city near whose airport the movement began.
“Blessing” — the movement’s claim to a fresh outpouring of the Spirit.
Tested by “decently and in order” and the fruit of self-control.
“Try the spirits whether they are of God” — the rule for all such claims.
Allied with later experience-driven charismatic movements.
usage: The Toronto Blessing is cited as a case of experience divorced from the Word.
Its phenomena are tested by the Spirit’s fruit of order and self-control.
It illustrates the duty to try the spirits rather than trust intensity of feeling.

etymology: From fundamentalist (one holding the fundamentals of the faith) and modernist (one accommodating the faith to modern thought); the great early twentieth-century battle in the American churches.
biblical_def: The Fundamentalist-Modernist Controversy was the great conflict in the American Protestant churches in the early decades of the twentieth century, between those who held the historic fundamentals of the Christian faith and those who sought to accommodate Christianity to modern thought. The modernists, shaped by German higher criticism, Darwinian evolution, and a confidence in human progress, denied or reinterpreted the supernatural core of the faith—the inerrancy of Scripture, the virgin birth, the substitutionary atonement, the bodily resurrection, and the miracles of Christ—reducing Christianity to ethics and religious experience. The fundamentalists, named from a series of essays called The Fundamentals, contended for these very doctrines as essential and non-negotiable. The conflict came to a head in the great denominations, especially the Presbyterian and Baptist churches of the North, where J. Gresham Machen wrote his clear and powerful Christianity and Liberalism, arguing that liberalism was not a variety of Christianity at all but a different religion under a Christian name. The dictionary judges the controversy with the fundamentalists in its essence, for they contended earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints against a modernism that hollowed out the gospel. It honors Machen’s diagnosis as exactly right: a religion that denies the supernatural Christ of the Scriptures is not a development of Christianity but its abandonment. The same battle continues wherever the church is tempted to trade the inspired Word and the supernatural gospel for the approval of the age.
webster_summary: The early twentieth-century battle in the American churches between those holding the historic fundamentals of the faith and modernists accommodating Christianity to higher criticism and evolution.
webster_full: FUNDAMENTALIST-MODERNIST CONTROVERSY, the early twentieth-century battle in the American churches.
Modernists, shaped by higher criticism and evolution, denied the supernatural core of the faith.
Fundamentalists contended for inerrancy, the virgin birth, the atonement, and the resurrection.
Came to a head in the Northern Presbyterian and Baptist churches.
J. Gresham Machen’s Christianity and Liberalism named liberalism a different religion.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain.
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
corruption_summary: Modernism hollowed out the gospel, denying the supernatural Christ while keeping the Christian name—a different religion, as Machen showed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption was modernism, also called liberalism—the program of accommodating Christianity to modern thought by denying its supernatural core. Shaped by higher-critical assumptions about the Bible, by evolutionary confidence, and by faith in human progress, the modernists reinterpreted away the inerrancy of Scripture, the virgin birth, the penal atonement, and the bodily resurrection, leaving an ethical and experiential religion with the supernatural Christ removed. Paul’s anathema falls on any other gospel; and a gospel without the risen Christ, Paul says, is preaching in vain.

Machen’s diagnosis remains the dictionary’s judgment: liberalism is not a variety of Christianity but a distinct religion wearing a Christian name. The fundamentalists, for all the caricatures later attached to the word, were right in the essential matter—they earnestly contended for the faith once delivered to the saints against those who would surrender it to the spirit of the age. The same controversy recurs in every generation, wherever the church is pressed to trade the inspired Word and the supernatural gospel for the approval of the world. The faithful answer is Jude’s: to contend for the faith once delivered, holding fast the supernatural Christ of the Scriptures.
roots_summary: The controversy named the line between the historic faith and a modernism that surrendered its supernatural core.
roots_lines: “The Fundamentals” — the essays from which the fundamentalists took their name.
“Modernism” / “liberalism” — the accommodation of the faith to modern thought.
Higher criticism — the German scholarship undermining Scripture’s authority.
J. Gresham Machen — author of Christianity and Liberalism.
The non-negotiables: inerrancy, virgin birth, atonement, resurrection, miracles.
usage: The Fundamentalist-Modernist Controversy is studied as the great battle over the supernatural gospel.
Machen’s thesis that liberalism is a different religion is widely cited.
It is applied to every renewal of the pressure to accommodate the faith to the age.

etymology: From Anglo (English) and Catholicism; the High-Church movement within Anglicanism stressing its continuity with medieval Catholicism.
biblical_def: Anglo-Catholicism is the High-Church movement within Anglicanism, springing chiefly from the Oxford Movement of the nineteenth century under Newman, Pusey, and Keble, which sought to recover for the Church of England the doctrines, ceremonies, and authority of pre-Reformation Catholicism. Reacting against both rationalism and low-church evangelicalism, the Tractarians stressed the apostolic succession of bishops, the priestly and sacrificial character of the ministry, baptismal regeneration, the real presence in the Eucharist, auricular confession, prayers for the dead, devotion to Mary and the saints, and an elaborate ceremonial. It represents a deliberate movement back toward Rome in doctrine and worship, and indeed Newman, its most famous leader, ended by submitting to the Roman Church. Measured against the Reformation, Anglo-Catholicism is a partial undoing of the recovery the English Reformers achieved at the cost of their blood—a reversal of the very corrections that called the church away from sacerdotalism, the cult of the saints, and the mass. The dictionary judges Anglo-Catholicism by the gospel the Reformation recovered: justification by faith alone, the sufficiency of Scripture, the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ, and the priesthood of all believers. It honors whatever in the movement reverenced the holiness of God and the dignity of worship, while naming its sacerdotal and Romeward doctrines as a corruption of the biblical gospel. The English martyrs died to deliver the church from precisely the errors the movement sought to restore.
webster_summary: The High-Church Anglican movement from the Oxford Movement, recovering pre-Reformation doctrine, sacrifice, and ceremony—a partial undoing of the English Reformation toward Rome.
webster_full: ANGLO-CATHOLICISM, the High-Church movement within Anglicanism.
Sprang chiefly from the Oxford Movement under Newman, Pusey, and Keble.
Recovered apostolic succession, sacrificial priesthood, baptismal regeneration, and Marian devotion.
A deliberate movement back toward Rome; Newman ended in the Roman Church.
A partial undoing of the recovery the English Reformers achieved.
scriptures: Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
corruption_summary: Anglo-Catholicism restores the sacerdotalism, the mass, and the cult of the saints the Reformation called the church away from.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the restoration of the very errors the English Reformation corrected. By reviving the sacrificing priesthood, the real presence understood as a re-offering, baptismal regeneration, auricular confession, prayers for the dead, and devotion to Mary and the saints, Anglo-Catholicism reverses the Reformation’s recovery of the gospel. Scripture answers each: a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law; by one offering Christ has perfected for ever them that are sanctified, so there is no continuing sacrifice; there is one Mediator between God and men; and all believers are a royal priesthood.

The dictionary honors what is honorable—the movement’s reverence for the holiness of God, its care for worship, and the personal devotion of many in it—while naming its sacerdotal and Romeward doctrines plainly as a corruption of the biblical gospel. The Oxford Movement’s logic carried Newman himself to Rome, which is where its principles lead. The English Reformers—Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley—went to the stake to deliver the church from the mass and the cult of the saints; to restore those very things is to undo their costly work and to obscure the finished work of Christ and the free justification of the sinner by faith alone.
roots_summary: The name marks an English Catholicism within Anglicanism, recovering Roman doctrine and reversing the Reformation.
roots_lines: “Anglo” — English; the movement is within the Church of England.
“Catholicism” — here the recovery of pre-Reformation Roman doctrine and worship.
The Oxford Movement and its Tracts for the Times (the Tractarians).
Sacerdotalism — the priestly, sacrificial view of the ministry it revived.
Newman’s conversion to Rome shows the movement’s logical end.
usage: Anglo-Catholicism is identified as the High-Church, Romeward movement in Anglicanism.
Its sacerdotal doctrines are answered by the Reformation’s recovered gospel.
The English martyrs are cited against restoring the errors they died to overthrow.

etymology: From Wesleyan (of John Wesley) and holiness; the tradition of sanctification teaching arising from Wesley and developed in the later Holiness movement.
biblical_def: Wesleyan holiness is the tradition of teaching on sanctification arising from John Wesley and developed in the nineteenth-century Holiness movement, distinguished by its doctrine of entire sanctification or Christian perfection—the claim that a believer may, by a definite second work of grace after conversion, be so cleansed from sin as to be made perfect in love in this life. Wesley taught that this perfection was not absolute sinlessness nor freedom from infirmity and mistake, but a heart wholly devoted to God and emptied of the conscious motions of sin against love; later Holiness teachers often pressed it further toward a doctrine of an instantaneous cleansing from the sin nature. The dictionary honors Wesley’s genuine zeal for holiness, his warm preaching of the new birth, and his rebuke of the dead formalism of his day, while marking his sanctification doctrine as a serious departure from the biblical and Reformed understanding. Scripture presents sanctification as a progressive, lifelong work, never complete in this life: the flesh lusts against the Spirit so that the believer cannot do all that he would; the most mature saints, like Paul, confess themselves chief of sinners and reach forth to what is still before; and the man who says he has no sin deceives himself. The dictionary holds that perfection is the believer’s goal, attained only at glorification, not a second blessing to be claimed now. The error of Wesleyan perfectionism, however earnest, breeds either pride in those who think they have attained, or despair in those who know they have not.
webster_summary: The tradition from John Wesley and the Holiness movement teaching entire sanctification or Christian perfection by a second work of grace—a departure from the biblical doctrine of progressive, lifelong sanctification.
webster_full: WESLEYAN HOLINESS, the sanctification tradition from Wesley and the Holiness movement.
Teaches entire sanctification or Christian perfection by a second work of grace.
Wesley meant a heart wholly devoted to God, not absolute sinlessness.
Later teachers pressed toward an instantaneous cleansing from the sin nature.
A departure from the biblical doctrine of progressive, lifelong sanctification.
scriptures: Gal 5:17
For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would.
Php 3:12
Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus.

corruption_summary: The doctrine of entire sanctification claims a perfection in this life that Scripture reserves for glory, breeding pride or despair.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the doctrine of perfectionism—the claim that the believer may be entirely sanctified, cleansed from indwelling sin, and made perfect in this present life by a second work of grace. Scripture teaches otherwise: the flesh lusts against the Spirit so that the believer cannot do the good he would; Paul, late in his course, denies that he is already perfect and presses on toward the goal; and John says that the man who claims to have no sin deceives himself. Sanctification is real and progressive, but its completion awaits glorification.

The dictionary honors Wesley’s burning zeal for holiness and his recovery of the new birth against the dead religion of his age, and acknowledges that he carefully qualified his doctrine. But the doctrine itself, and still more its later developments, departs from the biblical and Reformed understanding, and bears bitter practical fruit. Those who believe they have attained sinless perfection are tempted to pride and self-deception, redefining sin downward to fit their experience; those who honestly know the remaining corruption of their hearts are driven to despair of a perfection they cannot reach. The dictionary holds the surer doctrine: the believer wars against sin all his days, grows in grace progressively, and is made perfect only when he sees Christ and is made like Him.
roots_summary: The tradition’s name binds Wesley’s legacy to the pursuit of holiness, but its perfectionism departs from progressive sanctification.
roots_lines: “Wesleyan” — from John Wesley, founder of the Methodist movement.
“Entire sanctification” / “Christian perfection” — the second-blessing doctrine.
“Second work of grace” — a definite experience after conversion.
Set against the Reformed doctrine of progressive, lifelong sanctification.
Allied with the later nineteenth-century Holiness movement.
usage: Wesleyan holiness is identified by its doctrine of entire sanctification.
Its perfectionism is answered by the biblical doctrine of progressive sanctification.
Wesley’s zeal for holiness is honored while his sanctification doctrine is corrected.

etymology: The name of a prominent American author and former pastor associated with the emergent church and with universalist drift.
biblical_def: Rob Bell is a prominent American author and former megachurch pastor who became a leading voice of the so-called emergent church and, more seriously, of a universalist drift within popular evangelicalism. He came to wide attention through a series of stylish short films and books, and then to open controversy with his book Love Wins, which questioned the doctrine of eternal conscious punishment and suggested that the love of God will, in the end, embrace and save all—a revival of the old universalist hope under a modern, marketable form. In later years he moved further from historic Christianity, abandoning biblical teaching on sexuality and on the authority of Scripture, and drifting toward a vague spirituality. The dictionary names Rob Bell as a representative of progressive evangelicalism and universalist drift, and measures his teaching by the Word. Scripture is plain that the punishment of the wicked is eternal and conscious: the same word describes the everlasting life of the righteous and the everlasting punishment of the cursed; the smoke of their torment ascendeth for ever and ever; the rich man lifted up his eyes in torment. The love of God is real and infinitely precious, but it does not abolish His justice nor empty hell; rather it is displayed supremely at the cross, where God’s love and justice meet, and is received only through repentance and faith. The dictionary holds that the denial of eternal punishment is a grievous error, however winsomely presented, and that to teach all will be saved is to contradict the Lord Jesus, who spoke more of hell than any other.
webster_summary: An American author and former pastor, a leading voice of the emergent church and of universalist drift; his book Love Wins questioned eternal punishment, contradicting the plain teaching of Christ.
webster_full: ROB BELL, an American author and former megachurch pastor.
A leading voice of the emergent church and of universalist drift in evangelicalism.
His book Love Wins questioned the doctrine of eternal conscious punishment.
Later abandoned biblical teaching on sexuality and the authority of Scripture.
A representative of progressive evangelicalism, measured and corrected by the Word.

corruption_summary: The denial of eternal punishment and the drift toward universalism contradict Christ, who spoke more of hell than any other.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the denial of eternal conscious punishment and the drift toward universalism—the hope that the love of God will at last save all and empty hell. Scripture forecloses it. The Lord Jesus, who spoke more of hell than any other, used the same word for the everlasting life of the righteous and the everlasting punishment of the wicked; Revelation says the smoke of their torment ascends for ever and ever; Paul speaks of everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord. To teach that all will be saved is not a deeper grasp of love but a contradiction of the Saviour’s own words.

The dictionary names Rob Bell’s teaching, and the broader progressive evangelicalism he represents, as a grievous error, however winsomely packaged. The love of God is real and is the wonder of the gospel, but it does not abolish His justice; it is displayed not by emptying hell but by the cross, where Christ bore the wrath that justice required, so that all who repent and believe are saved and those who refuse perish justly. A “love” that sets aside God’s holiness and the warnings of Christ is not the love of the Bible. The dictionary holds the hard and merciful truth together: hell is real and eternal, the cross is the measure of God’s love, and salvation is received through repentance and faith alone.
roots_summary: The name stands for progressive evangelicalism and universalist drift, measured against the plain teaching of Christ on hell.
roots_lines: Love Wins — his book questioning eternal conscious punishment.
The “emergent church” — the movement with which he was associated.
Universalism — the ancient error, revived, that all will at last be saved.
Greek aiōnios — everlasting; used alike of life and of punishment in Matthew 25:46.

usage: Rob Bell is cited as a representative of universalist drift in popular evangelicalism.
Love Wins is answered by Christ’s own teaching on eternal punishment.
The love and justice of God are held together against emptying hell.

etymology: The Latinized name of the British-born monk and theologian of the late fourth and early fifth centuries, opponent of Augustine.
biblical_def: Pelagius was a British-born monk and moral teacher of the late fourth and early fifth centuries who became the great opponent of Augustine and the father of the heresy that bears his name. Scandalized by what he saw as moral laxity, and reading Augustine’s prayer “give what thou commandest, and command what thou wilt” as an excuse for sin, Pelagius taught a doctrine of human ability that denied original sin and the necessity of grace. He held that Adam’s sin injured only Adam, not his posterity, so that every man is born innocent, with a free will fully able to choose good or evil; that men sin only by imitation, not by inherited corruption; that grace is helpful but not necessary, an aid to what the will can in principle do without it; and that men may, by their own free choice and effort, keep the law of God and merit salvation. Augustine answered him decisively from Scripture, and Pelagianism was condemned as heresy by the councils of the church. The dictionary names Pelagianism as the archetypal denial of the gospel of grace, the doctrine that man can save himself. Scripture teaches the opposite at every point: in Adam all die, all have sinned, the natural man is dead in trespasses, no man is justified by the deeds of the law, and salvation is by grace through faith, not of works, lest any man should boast. Pelagius is remembered as the perennial type of every scheme—ancient or modern—that flatters human ability and denies the sinner’s helpless need of sovereign grace.
webster_summary: The British monk and opponent of Augustine who denied original sin and the necessity of grace, teaching that man by free will can keep God’s law and merit salvation—condemned as heresy.
webster_full: PELAGIUS, the British monk and theologian, opponent of Augustine.

Taught that men sin by imitation, not inherited corruption.
Held grace to be helpful but not necessary; man may merit salvation by effort.
Condemned as a heretic by the councils of the church.

Eph 2:8

corruption_summary: Pelagianism denies original sin and the necessity of grace, teaching that man can save himself by free will and effort.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is Pelagianism—the doctrine that man, unfallen in nature, can by his own free will keep God’s law and earn salvation, with grace a mere help rather than a necessity. Scripture denies it root and branch: by one man sin entered the world and death passed upon all, for that all have sinned; the natural man is dead in trespasses; the Ethiopian cannot change his skin nor the sinner do good who is accustomed to evil; and salvation is by grace through faith, the gift of God, not of works, lest any should boast. Pelagius makes man his own saviour and grace superfluous, overthrowing the gospel.

The dictionary names Pelagianism the archetypal denial of grace, condemned by the early church and refuted by Augustine, whose recovery of the biblical doctrine the Reformers gladly claimed. Its semi-Pelagian and Arminian descendants soften but do not cure the error, still granting fallen man a decisive ability and crediting salvation partly to the human will. The dictionary holds the doctrines of grace against them all: man is dead and helpless in sin, salvation is wholly of the Lord, regeneration precedes and produces faith, and the glory of the sinner’s rescue belongs to God alone. Pelagius stands as the perennial type of every flattering scheme of human ability and self-salvation.
roots_summary: His name marks the archetypal heresy of self-salvation—the denial of original sin and the necessity of grace.
roots_lines: Pelagianism — the heresy of human ability and self-salvation that bears his name.
Denied peccatum originale, original sin inherited from Adam.
Held the will liberum and able, needing grace only as a help.
Opposed by Augustine, the great doctor of grace.
Semi-Pelagianism and Arminianism are its softer descendants.
usage: Pelagius is named as the father of the heresy of self-salvation.
